newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Bangui civilians begin to return home, truce holds.
newsitem.headline: Bangui civilians begin to return home, truce holds.

text.p: Civilians who fled the Central African Republic capital in fear of their lives trickled back home on Monday as a truce in clashes between African peacekeepers and army dissidents held, aid workers said.

The head of the local Red Cross, David Dofara, told Reuters about 6,000 of the 60,000 people who took refugee in surrounding countryside had returned home but he highlighted problems with malaria and diarrhoea among those still displaced.

Officials said Mali's widely respected former military leader, Amadou Toumani Toure, pressed ahead with his efforts to extend a four-day truce and relaunch a January peace deal he negotiated to end three army mutinies in under a year.
The truce ends in theory on at 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) on Wednesday but the aim was to extend it.

The clashes, which have killed around 100 people, many of them civilians, began on June 20 after an incident between peacekeepers and disaffected soldiers among the minority who had yet to rejoin their units under the January deal.
Under the truce, the dissident soldiers were to hand mortars and other heavy weapons over to France's ambassador.
President Ange-Felix Patasse, the mutineers and representatives of all political groups and society at large signed the January deal.

Mutinies in April and May 1996 began as pay protests but evolved into a bid to topple Patasse, a civilian from the north, elected in 1993. A third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.
Most of the mutineers are members of the Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.
Former colonial power France has troops in the country under a defence pact. It intervened to restore order in January and then handed over to the peacekeepers.
